cim: FEC data: AI-oriented PACs spent nearly $80M on the 2026 US elections, mostly before the primaries; pro-regulatory PACs outspent Leading the Future's network (Ian Krietzberg/Puck)
cim_eredeti: FEC data: AI-oriented PACs spent nearly $80M on the 2026 US elections, mostly before the primaries; pro-regulatory PACs outspent Leading the Future's network (Ian Krietzberg/Puck)
szoveg_eredeti:
Since its launch in 2025, the pro-A.I. super PAC Leading the Future seemed poised to engage in a massive spending war for its preferred candidates—and with little opposition. Armed with more than $100 million in funding from Silicon Valley stalwarts including Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and Greg Brockman, the group spent the year pouring millions into primary campaigns across the country, a strategy that culminated in its deployment of an $8 million money bomb to bring down Alex Bores’s congressional campaign—a success, despite the millions more that had been deployed in support of the candidate.Those pro-Bores dollars came from a slate of opponents to Leading the Future, all of which emerged after the pro-A.I. super PAC went live. The most significant of these entities was Public First, a super PAC funded largely by its dark-money 501(c)(4) arm. (Anthropic has given tens of millions to Public First, with apparent constraints preventing the use of that money in election spending. The rest of its donors are obscured.) At around the same time, the slate widened to include You Can Push Back and Dream NYC, both of which aligned themselves with Public First in its push for more rapid and stringent regulation of the A.I. industry. Over the summer, two other regulation-oriented PACs, the Guardrails Alliance and Tomorrow Together, entered the picture.All told, this mix of A.I.-oriented PACs has spent just shy of $80 million on the 2026 elections, according to a comprehensive review of F.E.C. data. About three-quarters of this spending occurred before the primaries. “It is clear that there are two sides to this fight,” Shaunna Thomas, the co-founder and executive director of Guardrails, told me when we caught up on Wednesday morning. “You’re either on the side of Big A.I., or you’re on the side of the American public.” (Leading the Future has consistently stated it is not anti-regulation and simply supports a clear national standard.)Meanwhile, many pro-industry groups appear to have entered a strategic retreat. Amid public backlash against data center construction and broad skepticism toward A.I., Leading the Future has deployed only about $9 million between July and late October, spending only in support of candidates and mostly steering clear of the more hotly contested races. As of the last filing period, Team Safety actually ended up outspending Leading the Future’s network—$40 million to $36 million, per F.E.C. data. According to an industry source familiar with the situation, this apparent evolution is a strategic “feature, not a bug.” Strategists recognized that transforming A.I. into an overly partisan issue would be likely to backfire among the electorate, and presumably antagonize the very Democrats who will control the next Congress.For the pro-A.I. lobbying movement, coalition-building became more important. OpenAI C.E.O. Sam Altman acknowledged as much in a conversation with Politico earlier this month. “Something’s clearly not working,” he said. “I don’t think spending money on politics is what’s going to make people feel better about it.” Brockman and his wife, Anna, for instance, backed out of a $25 million contribution to Leading the Future, according to a September New York Times report. Meta retreated as well, with political groups it had funded returning some $25 million to the tech giant in recent weeks, according to state and I.R.S. filings.Meanwhile, the pro-safety contingent has ramped up its spending and largely become more aggressive, hitting back in nearly all of the races where Leading the Future had sought to tip the scales. Moreover, some of these groups are trying to make pro-industry endorsements a liability for candidates in races across the country. “It’s important in this general to demonstrate that not only is Leading the Future, or other anti-regulation PAC spending, toxic for the candidates they come in for, but that there’s a playbook to beat them,” Thomas told me. Leading the Future declined a request for comment.In the final sprint of the election, she explained, Guardrails is focusing on races where Leading the Future either issued endorsements or spent in the primary, “because they have essentially pulled out of most competitive races, or they’re spending really late to avoid our strategy, which is using their spending against the candidates they come in for.” In California, for instance, Democrat Jimmy Gomez has “refused to distance himself from Leading the Future’s endorsement,” Thomas said. “I think that’s going to play a role in him losing.”
